title: Cosmic Treasure Chest
caption: The globular cluster Terzan 9, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Stars are strewn so thickly across this Hubble image that it looks like a sea of sequins, or a treasure chest overflowing with gold. At its heart is Terzan 9, a globular cluster in Sagittarius, in the direction of the Milky Way's centre.

Globular clusters are stable, tightly bound gatherings of anywhere from tens of thousands to millions of stars, and their cores can be extremely crowded, as in Terzan 9. Hubble recorded the scene with two cameras, Wide Field Camera 3 and the Advanced Camera for Surveys.

The picture is part of a Hubble programme looking at globular clusters towards our galaxy's heart. That central region holds a dense crowd of stars called the Galactic bulge, which is also full of dust. The dust has long made nearby clusters hard to study, because it soaks up starlight and can shift the apparent colours of their stars. By observing in both visible and infrared light, Hubble lets astronomers measure how much the dust has altered those colours, and so work out the clusters' ages.

understand.summary: The image combines visible and near-infrared data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye and is less affected by dust, which is why it helps astronomers see clusters near the galactic centre.
